newsitem.title: AZERBAIJAN: Kazakh oil could go via underwater Caspian link.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh oil could go via underwater Caspian link.

text.p: A proposal to build an oil pipeline under the Caspian Sea to give Kazakhstan greater access to Western oil markets would not present special technical problems, energy officials said on Tuesday.
"This is still in the discussion stage," said Ilkham Aliyev, Vice-President of Azerbaijan's state oil company, SOCAR.
"But from the technical side, it shouldn't present any unique difficulties," he told reporters in the Azeri capital Baku.

A feasibility study authorised by Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan on the financial and technical aspects of the link should be complete by 1998, Baltabek Kuandykov, president of Kazakhstan's state-owned Kazakhstankaspiyshelf oil company, said.
"There should be no special technical problems with it," he said. "There are many, many precedents for underwater pipelines, such as in the North Sea."

The proposed pipeline would cross several hundred kilometres along the Caspian Sea floor from Kazakhstan to Azerbaijan and then perhaps link up with proposed and existing pipelines running from Azerbaijan to Western markets.
Neither Kuandykov or Aliyev could give any possible capacity figures, saying the project was still in an early stage.
Kuandykov was representing Kazakh Minister of Energy and Natural Resources Victor Kharpunov at the Fourth Annual International Caspian Oil & Gas Exhibition and Conference in Baku.
Kazakhkaspiyshelf represents Kazakhstan's state interests in a proposed consortium with Western oil firms to develop offshore Caspian fields.
The proposed consortium is being managed by Royal Dutch/Shell and includes Italy's Agip, British Gas, Mobil, Total S.A., and an alliance between British Petroleum and Norway's Statoil.

Kuandykov said that whether or not the undersea pipeline became a reality, ways had to be found to export crude from Kazakhstan, where output is expected to reach at least 120 million tonnes per year (2.4 million bpd) by 2015-2020.

"The most pessimistic estimates say that by 2015-2020, we will be producing 120 million tonnes (per year)," he said. "The most optimistic estimates say we will be producing 200 million tonnes (per year) (4 million bpd)."
"Even under the most pessimistic scenario, we will need to find alternate routes to export."
